hook.line: Vale has been tired all week, and she says so twice in one breath. One *-ado* word changes its ending for her; the other never does. Spot which.
hook.es: Estoy cansada. He estado cansada toda la semana.
hook.en: I'm tired. I've been tired all week. (a woman speaking)

examples.en: They haven't opened the shops yet.

examples.es: Todavía no he lavado las tazas.
examples.en: I haven't washed the cups yet.

examples.es: He estado cansada toda la semana.
examples.en: I've been tired all week. (a woman speaking)
Have you been ill this year? (to a woman friend)

rule:
The *-ado*, *-ido* word has two jobs, and they behave differently.

After *estar*, it describes, so it agrees: *la puerta está cerrada*, *las tiendas están cerradas*, *Vale está cansada*.

After *he*, *has*, *ha*, *hemos*, *han*, it's part of the verb, and it never changes. It stays *-o* whoever and whatever: *Todavía no han abierto las tiendas.* Never *abiertas*.

One quick test: look to its left.
*Estar* there: match the ending.
*He*, *has*, *ha*, *hemos* or *han* there: leave it alone.

That's why *he estado cansada* has one of each. *Estado* follows *he*, so it never changes; *cansada* describes Vale, so it agrees.
smallPrint: Teachers say the participle agrees when it works as an adjective and never changes inside a compound tense like the *pretérito perfecto*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *abierto* or *abierta*: Todavía no han ___ la droguería.
yourTurn.answer: Todavía no han abierto la droguería.
yourTurn.why: After *han*, it never changes, even with *la droguería*.

yourTurn.prompt: A woman says: I've been tired all week.
yourTurn.answer: He estado cansada toda la semana.
yourTurn.why: *Estado* follows *he* and stays put; *cansada* describes her.

yourTurn.prompt: Now say it as not yet: I haven't washed the cups yet.
yourTurn.answer: Todavía no he lavado las tazas.
accept: No he lavado las tazas todavía.

yourTurn.prompt: They haven't opened the shops yet. An hour later, say: The shops are open.
yourTurn.why: Now it's a state after *están*, so it agrees: *abiertas*.

pitfalls.wrong: Todavía no he lavadas las tazas.
pitfalls.right: Todavía no he lavado las tazas.
pitfalls.why: Almost. After *he*, the *-ado* word never changes, even with *las tazas*.
After *están*, it describes the shops, so it agrees: *cerradas*.
*Estado* follows *he*, so it stays *-o*. Only *cansada* describes you.

personal: Say how you are today with *estoy*, then something you haven't done yet this week with *todavía no he*.
